title: SLOs, error budgets, burn rates and profiling
seriesDescription: Logs, metrics, traces, SLOs, error budgets, burn rates and profiling. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: SLIs, SLOs and error budget arithmetic, multiwindow burn-rate alerts, Little's law capacity maths, and how to narrow down a slow endpoint with traces, flame graphs and off-CPU analysis.
source: Google SRE Book (Service Level Objectives) and SRE Workbook (Alerting on SLOs); Brendan Gregg on flame graphs and off-CPU analysis; Prometheus documentation (querying); Little's law

questions.prompt: An availability SLO of 99.9% is measured over a rolling 30-day window. How many seconds of full outage does the error budget allow?
questions.explanation: 30 days = 2,592,000 seconds. The budget is 0.1% of that, 2,592 seconds, which is 43.2 minutes.

questions.prompt: Match each availability SLO to the downtime it allows over a 30-day window (43,200 minutes).
questions.explanation: Budget = (1 - SLO) x 43,200 minutes. Each extra nine divides the budget by ten, which is why four nines is a very different engineering commitment from three.

questions.prompt: Your SLO is 99.9% of requests succeed. In the last hour 0.4% of requests failed. What is the burn rate (budget consumed relative to the sustainable pace)?
questions.explanation: Allowed error ratio is 0.1%. Observed 0.4% divided by 0.1% is a burn rate of 4: at this pace the 30-day budget is gone in 7.5 days.

questions.prompt: The Google SRE workbook example pages when the burn rate is at least 14.4 over 1 hour (and over 5 minutes). Why 14.4?

options.text: It is the 99.9% SLO value rewritten as a multiplier for the alert.
options.why: The SLO target does not appear in the multiplier; it comes from budget share and window.

options.text: At that rate 2% of a 30-day budget is spent in one hour.
It equals 24 hours divided by the 1.67 hour page window.
options.why: That is a coincidence of arithmetic, not the derivation.

options.text: It is an arbitrary vendor default with no maths behind it.
options.why: The number is derived from the budget share per window.

questions.explanation: The short second window (5 minutes) makes the alert reset quickly after the problem is fixed. Pair it with slower, lower-rate tickets (for example burn 1 over 3 days).

questions.prompt: The SLO is 99.9 percent over 30 days (720 hours). The error ratio runs at a burn rate of 6 for 6 hours. What percentage of the 30-day error budget has been consumed?
questions.explanation: Budget consumed = burn rate x window / period = 6 x 6 / 720 = 0.05, i.e. 5 percent. This is the SRE workbook's second paging tier (6x over 6 hours).

questions.prompt: Match each multiwindow burn-rate alert from the Google SRE workbook example (30-day SLO) with the share of the error budget it represents and the response.

right.text: 2 percent of the budget, page someone
5 percent of the budget, page someone
10 percent of the budget, open a ticket

questions.explanation: Each row is budget consumed = burn rate x window / 720 h: 14.4 x 1/720 = 2%, 6 x 6/720 = 5%, 1 x 72/720 = 10%. Fast burns page, slow burns file a ticket.

questions.prompt: Write the PromQL expression for the 1 hour error ratio of an HTTP service: the rate of `http_requests_total` with a `status` label matching `5xx`, divided by the rate of all `http_requests_total`, both summed over all series.
questions.explanation: Divide the burn alert threshold by the allowed error ratio (for example `error_ratio > 14.4 * 0.001`). Sum the rates first and divide afterwards so that low-traffic series do not dominate. Other label spellings (code, status_code) work equally well.

questions.prompt: An endpoint receives 200 requests per second and each request holds one DB connection for 250 ms on average. By Little's law, how many connections are in use on average?
questions.explanation: L = lambda x W = 200 x 0.25 = 50. Size the pool with headroom above this, and remember that a slowdown raises W and therefore exhausts the pool.

questions.prompt: A request needs two services in series, each with 99.9 percent availability and failing independently. What is the best-case combined availability in percent, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: 0.999 x 0.999 = 0.998001, about 99.8 percent. Dependencies in series multiply, so a service cannot promise a better SLO than the product of its hard dependencies unless it degrades gracefully.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Page on user-visible symptoms such as SLO burn rather than on causes such as high CPU.
questions.reason: Users only experience failures and latency, and a CPU spike may be harmless.

whys.a: Correct: Symptom alerts map to user pain; a cause metric can fire with no user impact.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Cause metrics are still useful on dashboards for diagnosis, just not as the main paging signal.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A team with plenty of unspent error budget can ship riskier changes faster.
questions.reason: The error budget equals one minus the SLO target.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Correct: Both are true, but the formula alone does not say what to do with unspent budget; the policy of spending it does.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: The budget turns reliability into a shared currency between product and operations.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A 100% availability SLO is the safest target for a customer-facing API.
questions.reason: Every dependency (network, cloud zone, deploys) can fail, so zero downtime cannot be promised.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Correct: A is false: it leaves no budget for deploys and costs far more than users can perceive. R is true.

questions.explanation: Pick the target users can actually notice and spend the remaining budget on change.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A latency SLO written on the 99th percentile describes user experience better than one written on the mean.
questions.reason: The arithmetic mean of a latency distribution always equals its median.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Correct: A is true because the mean hides the slow tail. R is false: a skewed distribution has a mean far above its median.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Report latency as the share of requests faster than a threshold (for example 99 percent under 300 ms) so it composes into a good-events ratio.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a well-formed service level indicator (SLI) for an API?

options.text: Average CPU utilisation measured across the whole fleet of servers at once.
options.why: CPU is a cause metric, not what users experience.

options.text: Good events over valid events, such as fast non-5xx responses.
options.why: Correct: a ratio of good to valid events maps directly to an SLO percentage.

options.text: The number of pods that are currently running in the production cluster.
options.why: Pod count describes capacity, not service quality.

options.text: Mean time between production deployments, measured over the last quarter.
options.why: Deployment frequency is a delivery metric, not a service level.

questions.explanation: Pick the measurement point (load balancer or client), define 'good' (status and latency threshold) and 'valid' (exclude health checks and caller errors), then set the SLO target on that ratio.

questions.text: In a flame graph the {1} of a frame shows its share of samples, and stack depth runs along the {2} axis.
questions.explanation: Colours are usually arbitrary; the horizontal order is alphabetical, not time.

questions.prompt: `GET /reports` is slow only in production. What is the best first step?

options.text: Look at a trace of a slow request to see which span dominates.
options.why: Correct: a trace narrows the time to a stage before any tool is chosen.

options.text: Rewrite the whole service logic in a faster language straight away.
options.why: A rewrite without measurement may not touch the real bottleneck.

options.text: Double the pod count and see whether it helps with the slow requests.
options.why: Adding capacity does not help if the wait is in a lock, a query or a remote call.

options.text: Turn on `DEBUG` logging for the entire production cluster at once.
options.why: Mass debug logging adds load and noise without locating the stage.

questions.explanation: Measure, narrow to a stage (DB, remote call, CPU, lock wait), then use the matching tool: `EXPLAIN` for SQL, a profiler for CPU, stack dumps for waiting.

questions.prompt: p99 latency is 5 s but CPU sits at 15% and p50 is fine. A CPU profile shows nothing hot. What kind of problem do you suspect?

options.text: A tight loop in business code burning cores for most requests.
options.why: A hot loop would raise CPU use and show up in the profile.

options.text: A JSON payload that is too small for the serializer to handle.
options.why: Payload size cannot be too small to cause a multi-second wait.

options.text: Time spent waiting off CPU: locks, pool queues, I/O or pauses.
options.why: Correct: waiting does not show in a CPU profile.

options.text: An overly verbose class name making stack traces hard to read.

questions.explanation: Off-CPU time is invisible to a CPU profile. Wall-clock sampling and repeated stack dumps expose waiting; a saturated connection-pool queue is a frequent culprit.
